Flow diagram of traditional gari processing. Six steps connected by arrows. 1. A woman peeling fresh cassava tubers with a knife. 2. Washing peeled tubers in a bowl of water. 3. Grating the tubers into a mash. 4. A jute sack of cassava mash squeezed under heavy stones to drain water (fermentation and pressing). 5. Sieving the mash through a locally woven sieve. 6. Roasting the sieved mash in a wide shallow cast-iron pan over a wood fire to produce dry gari.

A traditional yam barn. A vertical framework made of growing wooden poles (live poles) with horizontal wooden crossbars. Large yam tubers are tied individually to the framework using ropes. The structure is shaded by the leaves of the live poles.

A rectangular farm structure known as a maize crib. It has a wooden framework raised on stilt legs about 1 metre off the ground. On each leg is a downward-pointing metal cone (a rat guard). The walls are made of wire mesh to allow wind to blow through. The crib is filled with yellow maize on the cob. It has a sloped corrugated iron roof to protect from rain.

A tall, cylindrical modern metal silo used for bulk grain storage. It has a conical roof and a conical bottom for easy discharge. An access ladder runs up the side. Beside it is a smaller intake pipe and a tractor with a trailer unloading grain into a hopper.
